hints: Focus on what temperature really means for molecules, it controls their average kinetic energy.
Think about the shape change when heated, the curve flattens and spreads out because fewer molecules stay at low energy.
Remember activation energy is an energy value on the x-axis, while X and Y are vertical heights showing proportion of molecules.
walkthrough:
**Read the Boltzmann axes**

Think of this curve as showing how energy is shared out. The x-axis is molecular energy $E$, the y-axis is proportion of molecules with that energy.

The peak is the most probable energy, and the total area under the curve is the total number of molecules.

**Predict the effect of higher temperature**

Heating gives molecules more energy on average. So the whole distribution shifts toward higher energy.

The peak gets lower and broader (flatter) because the same number of molecules is now spread over a wider energy range, and the maximum moves to the right to higher $E$.

**Check what X and Y really are**

X and Y are vertical arrows. They measure proportion (y-value), not energy.

Activation energy, $E_a$, would be a point marked along the horizontal $E$ axis, and enthalpy change, $\Delta H$, is not shown on this diagram at all.

options.A: Incorrect. Raising temperature spreads molecules over a wider energy range, so the peak height decreases, not increases. The total area must stay constant, so a broader curve must be shorter.
options.B: Correct. Higher temperature increases average molecular energy, so the most probable energy increases. The maximum flattens and shifts to the right to higher E.
options.C: Incorrect. Activation energy is a value of molecular energy $E$ on the x-axis. Line X is a tiny vertical height showing the very small proportion of molecules with very high energy, not the $E_a$ value itself.
options.D: Incorrect. Line Y is the vertical height of the peak, showing the proportion of molecules with the most probable energy. Enthalpy change is an energy difference for a reaction and is never read as a y-height on a Boltzmann plot.
